hints.content: Read the statement again and point at the single term that changed between one line and the next.
Write down what variables and expressions gives you and what it asks for, on separate lines, before doing any arithmetic.
Replace x with a small number such as 2 and see what each side of the statement becomes.
Check the sign of every term you moved. A term that crosses the equals sign changes sign; a term that does not, does not.
Deal with the terms that do not contain x first, then the coefficient multiplying x.
Try variables and expressions on two different values of x and compare. If both give the same answer, the step you took did not depend on x at all.
Test your rule on a case designed to break it, such as a negative coefficient or a zero constant, and see whether it still holds.
Think of the equation as a balance: whatever you do to one side must happen to the other, or the two sides stop describing the same number.
Write the rule for variables and expressions as a general statement in letters first, then substitute your numbers into it.
Suppose your answer were right. Substitute it back into the original statement and carry the arithmetic through. Where the two sides disagree is where the rule broke.
Trace variables and expressions back to arithmetic you already trust: the same rule holds when every letter is replaced by a number, and the letters only record that it holds for all of them at once.
Work one full example of variables and expressions line by line, writing beside each line which rule let you move from the line above.
